output.answer: Yes. Most recently, on Oct. 14, 2026, The Washington Post said it would lay off more than 100 workers — press operators, machinists and circulation drivers, some union-represented — as it closes its Springfield, Va. printing plant. That followed the paper's largest layoff of the year on Feb. 4, 2026, when it cut roughly one-third of its staff, eliminating its sports section, several foreign bureaus and its books coverage (over 300 newsroom journalists, plus about 75 people from its Arc XP software arm); publisher/CEO Will Lewis stepped down days later. The Post has since quietly rehired a small number of the laid-off staffers into new roles.
caveats: The exact total number of Feb. 2026 layoffs was never officially confirmed: the Post did not publish an official headcount, and figures like 'one-third of staff' and 'over 300 journalists' come from the AP and via the Status newsletter as reported by the NY Post.
Some laid-off staffers have been rehired, so the current net headcount reduction is smaller than the February cuts implied; the Post did not say how many accepted return offers.

The Springfield plant layoff figure ('more than 100 workers') is from a Washington Business Journal report; the article's detailed body was behind a subscriber wall, so the precise count and timing of the plant closure could shift.

output.question: Has The Washington Post announced layoffs?

key_facts.fact: The Washington Post said it would lay off more than 100 workers as it closes its Springfield, Va. printing plant; affected workers include press operators, machinists, circulation drivers and others, some union-represented.

The Washington Post laid off one-third of its staff on Feb. 4, 2026, eliminating its sports section, several foreign bureaus and its books coverage — a purge affecting virtually every newsroom department.

The Feb. 2026 cuts impacted roughly 30% of the Post's staff, including hundreds from the newsrooms and around 75 people from Arc XP, its software services arm; the Guild said the workforce had already shrunk by roughly 400 people over three years.
Washington Post publisher/CEO Will Lewis stepped down days after the mass layoffs (his resignation was reported Feb. 9, 2026).

After the February cuts eliminated over 300 newsroom jobs, the Post quietly began rehiring some laid-off staffers into new roles, including at least 10 contacted about returning and several who accepted.
Earlier, in May 2025, the Post announced voluntary buyouts for staffers with 10 or more years of service, a process it said would conclude by end of July 2025.
